name: Columbus 2050
summary: Fly down the Scioto and along Broad Street through one possible, greener future for downtown Columbus.
description: An artistic future scenario for downtown Columbus, Ohio, built on real geography from OpenStreetMap: today's streets, building footprints, the Scioto River and parks, with the LeVeque Tower and the Ohio Statehouse modelled on their real footprints. The imagined 2050 layer adds green and solar roofs, rapid transit in green lanes on Broad and High streets, protected bike lanes, street trees and a riverbank forest, autonomous electric shuttles, a rooftop vertiport, a green footbridge, and mass-timber towers and a solar microgrid on what are surface parking lots today.

geo.note: Origin (0,0) is High St & Broad St; metres; x east, z south.

learningObjectives: See how a restored river, parks and street trees can cool a city and handle stormwater.
Compare ways to move people downtown: transit, bikes, walking, shared electric vehicles and air taxis.
Notice how buildings can produce clean energy and store it nearby.

status.notes: Real streets, buildings and river from OpenStreetMap; the 2050 additions are imagined. Most building heights are estimated from building type.

disclaimer: Columbus 2050 is an artistic future scenario, not an official plan.

display.title: COLUMBUS 2050
display.author: AN ARTISTIC SCENARIO
display.themeLine: Rivers, trees, transit and clean energy: a city designed to sustain life.

hotspots.label: Scioto River
hotspots.title: The Scioto River, running free
hotspots.text: Downtown's river used to sit behind a low dam. The Scioto Greenways project removed the Main Street dam, narrowed the river and turned old riverbed into parkland. In this 2050 scenario an urban forest lines both banks.

facts.text: About 1.06 miles of the Scioto were returned to free-flowing condition, and the river's width through downtown was cut roughly in half.
facts.source: Landscape Architecture Foundation, Scioto Mile & Greenways case study

facts.text: Removing the dam and floodwalls reclaimed about 33 acres of open space; Greenways was completed in November 2015.

hotspots.archive: A river with room to breathe, and a forest along both banks.

question.q: What happened when the Main Street dam was removed?
options: The river got wider and deeper
The river narrowed and new parkland appeared
question.why: Without the dam the river returned to a narrower, free-flowing channel, and the land it used to cover became parks.

hotspots.label: Vertiport
hotspots.title: A rooftop vertiport
hotspots.text: An imagined mobility hub: buses, bikes and shared electric vehicles on the ground floor, solar panels on the roof, and pads where small electric air taxis land and take off.

facts.text: eVTOL stands for electric vertical take-off and landing: aircraft that rise straight up like a helicopter but run on batteries.

hotspots.archive: Air taxis, buses and bikes, all meeting in one place.

question.q: Why put a vertiport on top of a transit hub?
options: So people can switch between air taxis, buses and bikes in one place
Because air taxis need to land on buses
question.why: Hubs make it easy to change modes, so one trip can combine several kinds of transport.

hotspots.label: Green Bridge
hotspots.title: A bridge for people, not cars
hotspots.text: This imagined bridge carries only people walking, rolling and biking, with trees planted along it for shade.

facts.text: Shaded surfaces can be 20–45°F cooler than the peak temperatures of unshaded surfaces.
facts.source: U.S. EPA, Using Trees and Vegetation to Reduce Heat Islands

hotspots.archive: A bridge just for walking and biking, with shade trees.

question.q: How do trees cool a street?
options: They shade surfaces and release water vapor from their leaves
They reflect heat back into the sky like mirrors
question.why: Shade keeps the sun off pavement, and evapotranspiration from leaves cools the air.

hotspots.label: LeVeque Tower
hotspots.title: LeVeque Tower (1927)
hotspots.text: The Art Deco LeVeque Tower opened in 1927 and was the tallest building in Ohio when it was finished. It is kept here as it is today: the future is built around the city's history, not instead of it.

facts.text: It was the tallest building in Ohio when it opened in 1927.

hotspots.archive: The LeVeque Tower, 1927. Still standing tall.

hotspots.label: Scioto Mile
hotspots.title: The Scioto Mile
hotspots.text: A chain of riverfront parks, paths and fountains along downtown's edge. Bicentennial Park's fountain is a favorite summer spot.

facts.text: The Scioto Mile parks were completed in June 2011.

hotspots.label: Rapid transit
hotspots.title: Rapid transit on Broad Street
hotspots.text: In this scenario, rapid-transit vehicles run every few minutes in their own green lanes down the middle of Broad and High streets, with protected bike lanes on both sides. This is an artistic picture, not COTA's actual design.

facts.text: COTA's LinkUS program is planning bus rapid transit on West Broad Street, about 9 miles from Downtown to Prairie Township with 17 new stations.
In 2024 the West Broad corridor received a $42 million federal grant.

hotspots.archive: Rapid transit in its own green lane. No traffic jams.

question.q: Why give transit its own lane?
options: So it doesn't get stuck in car traffic, making trips faster and more reliable
Because buses are too wide for normal lanes
question.why: A dedicated lane keeps transit moving even when car traffic is heavy.

hotspots.label: Bike lanes
hotspots.title: Protected bike lanes everywhere
hotspots.text: Every street in this future has a green, protected lane for bikes and scooters, separated from cars, so short trips are easy without driving.
hotspots.archive: Green lanes for bikes on every street.

hotspots.label: Ohio Statehouse
hotspots.title: The Ohio Statehouse
hotspots.text: Ohio's capitol, a Greek Revival building with a flat-topped cupola instead of a dome, sits on Capitol Square at Broad and High.

facts.text: Construction began in 1839 and the building was completed in 1861.

hotspots.label: Green roofs
hotspots.title: Green roofs and rooftop solar
hotspots.text: Most roofs in this future are planted or covered in solar panels. Plants soak up rain and keep roofs cool; panels make electricity right where it is used.

facts.text: Green roofs absorb rainwater, which slows stormwater runoff, and they stay cooler than conventional roofs in summer.
facts.source: U.S. EPA, Using Green Roofs to Reduce Heat Islands

hotspots.archive: Green roofs and solar on nearly every building.

question.q: Which two jobs can a green roof do?
options: Hold rainwater and keep the building cooler
Make the building taller and heavier
question.why: Soil and plants store rain and shade the roof, cutting runoff and heat.

hotspots.label: Microgrid
hotspots.title: A neighborhood microgrid
hotspots.text: A battery hall stores solar power from nearby roofs and canopies. If the main grid goes down, the microgrid can keep key buildings running on its own.

facts.text: A microgrid is a local energy system that can connect to the main grid or disconnect and run on its own ('island mode').

hotspots.archive: Solar by day, stored for the night.

hotspots.label: Mass-timber towers
hotspots.title: Mass-timber towers
hotspots.text: Engineered wood such as cross-laminated timber can replace some concrete and steel. Wood keeps storing the carbon the tree took in while it grew. The planted setbacks hold trees and gardens.

facts.text: The 2021 International Building Code allows mass-timber buildings up to 18 stories tall.

hotspots.archive: Towers made of wood, with gardens on every step.

facts.text: Columbus 2050 is an artistic future scenario, not an official plan.
Streets, buildings and the river come from OpenStreetMap. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0.
Columbus was founded in 1812 on the banks of the Scioto River.
About 905,000 people lived in Columbus at the 2020 census.
The LeVeque Tower opened in 1927; the Ohio Statehouse was completed in 1861.
COTA's LinkUS program is planning bus rapid transit on West Broad Street.
